questions.q: Which DNS record maps a hostname to an IPv4 address?
questions.explain: A = IPv4, AAAA ('quad-A') = IPv6, MX = mail server, PTR = reverse lookup (IP → name), CNAME = alias.

questions.q: Which DNS record type maps a hostname to an IPv6 address?
questions.explain: AAAA. Four A's because an IPv6 address is four times longer than IPv4 (128 vs 32 bits).

questions.q: Which DNS record tells other mail servers where to deliver email for a domain?
questions.explain: MX (mail exchanger) records list mail servers with priorities. TXT holds text such as SPF policies; NS names the domain's authoritative DNS servers.

questions.q: www.netrealm.io should simply be an ALIAS of netrealm.github.io. Which record do you create?
questions.explain: A CNAME points one name at another canonical name. (You can't put a CNAME at the zone apex, which is why ALIAS/ANAME records exist.)

questions.q: Which record type is used for a REVERSE DNS lookup (IP address → name)?
questions.explain: PTR records live under in-addr.arpa (IPv4) or ip6.arpa (IPv6) and map addresses back to names.

questions.q: Order the four DHCP messages a client and server exchange (DORA).
questions.explain: Client broadcasts Discover → server Offers an address → client Requests it → server Acknowledges. Remember 'DORA'.

questions.q: How does a client send its initial DHCP Discover?
choices: As a broadcast, because it has no IP address yet
As a unicast to the DHCP server
questions.explain: The client uses source 0.0.0.0 and destination 255.255.255.255 (UDP 68 → 67). Broadcasts don't cross routers, which is why DHCP relay exists.

questions.q: What does `ip helper-address` do on a router interface?
choices: Relays DHCP broadcasts as unicast to a DHCP server on another subnet
questions.explain: It makes the router a DHCP relay agent: it catches the client's broadcast and forwards it to the server's IP. Configure it on the interface facing the clients.

questions.q: What is PAT (NAT overload)?
choices: Many inside hosts share one public IP, told apart by port numbers
One private IP permanently mapped to one public IP
questions.explain: PAT tracks (inside IP, inside port) ↔ (public IP, unique port). It's how a home router puts a whole house behind one ISP address.

questions.q: In Cisco NAT terminology, the PUBLIC address that represents an inside host to the outside world is the:
questions.explain: Inside local = the host's real (private) IP. Inside global = what the internet sees for that host. 'Local/global' = which side's point of view.

questions.q: Which kind of NAT gives an internal web server a permanent one-to-one public address?
questions.explain: Static NAT is a fixed 1:1 mapping, so outside users can reliably initiate connections to the server. Dynamic NAT uses a pool, and PAT shares one IP.

questions.q: A STANDARD IPv4 ACL can filter traffic based on:
choices: Source and destination IP, protocol and ports
questions.explain: Standard ACLs (1–99, 1300–1999) match only the source. Extended ACLs (100–199, 2000–2699) match source/destination, protocol and ports.

questions.q: General placement rule for ACLs?
choices: Extended ACLs close to the SOURCE; standard ACLs close to the DESTINATION
Standard close to the source; extended close to the destination
questions.explain: Extended ACLs are precise, so drop unwanted traffic early. Standard ACLs only see the source, so placing them near the source could block that source from everything.

questions.q: What sits invisibly at the end of every Cisco ACL?
questions.explain: Traffic that matches no line is dropped by the implicit deny. An ACL with only deny lines blocks everything! Add `permit any` where needed.

questions.q: Which numbered ACL range is for EXTENDED IPv4 ACLs?
questions.explain: Standard: 1–99, 1300–1999. Extended: 100–199, 2000–2699. Named ACLs avoid memorizing numbers.

questions.q: In NTP, what does a LOWER stratum number indicate?
choices: Closer to the reference clock (more authoritative)
questions.explain: Stratum 0 = reference clock (GPS, atomic). Stratum 1 servers attach directly to it, stratum 2 syncs from stratum 1, and so on. Accurate time matters for logs and certificates.

questions.q: In the CIA triad, ensuring data hasn't been altered in transit is:
questions.explain: Confidentiality = only authorized people can read it (encryption). Integrity = it hasn't been changed (hashes, MACs). Availability = it's there when needed (redundancy, anti-DDoS).

questions.q: In AAA, recording what commands a user ran and when is:
questions.explain: Authentication = who are you? Authorization = what may you do? Accounting = what did you do?

questions.q: Which AAA protocol encrypts the ENTIRE payload, runs over TCP 49 and separates authentication from authorization?
questions.explain: TACACS+ (Cisco, TCP 49) is great for device admin with per-command authorization. RADIUS (UDP 1812/1813) encrypts only the password and is common for network access.

questions.q: What is the DEFAULT violation mode for Cisco port security?
questions.explain: Shutdown err-disables the port. Restrict drops and logs offending frames; Protect silently drops them.

questions.q: With DHCP snooping enabled, which switch ports should be TRUSTED?
choices: Ports toward the legitimate DHCP server or uplinks
questions.explain: Untrusted ports may not send DHCP server messages (Offer/Ack), which kills rogue DHCP servers. Snooping also builds a binding table used by DAI and IP Source Guard.

questions.q: Dynamic ARP Inspection validates ARP packets against:
questions.explain: DAI drops ARP replies whose IP-to-MAC pairing doesn't match the DHCP snooping bindings (or static ARP ACLs). That stops ARP spoofing / MITM.

questions.q: WPA3-Personal replaces the WPA2 pre-shared key handshake with:
questions.explain: SAE (Dragonfly) resists offline dictionary attacks and provides forward secrecy. WPA3-Enterprise uses 802.1X.

questions.q: Which three 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi channels do NOT overlap (US)?
questions.explain: 2.4 GHz channels are 5 MHz apart but about 20–22 MHz wide, so only 1, 6 and 11 avoid overlapping in the US. 5 GHz has many more channels.

questions.q: Which band does 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5) use?
questions.explain: 802.11ac is 5 GHz only. 802.11n (Wi-Fi 4) is 2.4/5 GHz, 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) is 2.4/5 GHz, and Wi-Fi 6E adds 6 GHz.

questions.q: Wi-Fi 6 is the marketing name for which standard?
Which protocol suite is most commonly used for site-to-site VPNs across the internet?
questions.explain: IPsec gives confidentiality, integrity and authentication. GRE alone isn't encrypted, so it's often wrapped in IPsec (GRE over IPsec).

questions.q: Phishing carried out over voice phone calls is called:
questions.explain: Vishing = voice. Smishing = SMS. Whaling = phishing aimed at executives. Pharming = redirecting users to fake sites (e.g. DNS poisoning).

questions.q: What makes a DDoS different from a DoS?
choices: Traffic comes from many distributed sources (often a botnet)
questions.explain: Distributed denial of service: thousands of compromised devices attack at once, so blocking a single source IP doesn't help.

questions.q: An attacker sends fake ARP replies claiming to be the default gateway. What attack is this?
questions.explain: Victims send gateway traffic to the attacker, who can read or modify it. Defend with Dynamic ARP Inspection.

questions.q: Why should you use SSH instead of Telnet to manage devices?
choices: SSH encrypts the session, including passwords; Telnet is clear text
questions.explain: Anyone sniffing a Telnet session sees your password. Use `transport input ssh` on VTY lines.

questions.q: What does a STATEFUL firewall do that a simple packet filter does not?
choices: Tracks connections and automatically allows the return traffic
questions.explain: A stateful firewall keeps a session table, so replies to inside-initiated connections are allowed without wide-open inbound rules.

questions.q: What is a DMZ used for?
choices: Hosting public-facing servers in a zone separate from the internal LAN
questions.explain: Web, mail and DNS servers go in the DMZ. If one is compromised, the attacker still faces a firewall before reaching internal systems.

questions.q: A fingerprint scan is which MFA factor?
questions.explain: Know = password/PIN. Have = phone, hardware token. Are = biometrics. Real MFA combines DIFFERENT factor types.

questions.q: Which syslog severity level is the MOST severe?
questions.explain: Lower number = worse. 0 Emergency, 1 Alert, 2 Critical, 3 Error, 4 Warning, 5 Notice, 6 Informational, 7 Debugging.

questions.q: What does SNMPv3 add over v1/v2c?
questions.explain: v1/v2c use clear-text community strings. SNMPv3 adds users, authentication (authNoPriv) and encryption (authPriv).

questions.q: In an ACL, the keyword `host 10.1.1.5` is equivalent to which wildcard?
questions.explain: Wildcard 0.0.0.0 means every bit must match: one exact host. `any` = 0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255.

questions.q: What wildcard mask matches the subnet mask 255.255.255.240?
questions.explain: 255 − 240 = 15, so the wildcard is 0.0.0.15 (matches 16 addresses, a /28).

questions.q: Order the syslog severity levels from 0 (most severe) to 7.
questions.explain: Mnemonic: 'Every Awesome Cisco Engineer Will Need Ice cream Daily'.

questions.q: Order the steps of a full (uncached) DNS lookup for www.netrealm.io.
items: Resolver returns the answer and caches it (for the TTL)
questions.explain: Root servers point to TLD servers, TLD servers point to the authoritative servers, and the authoritative server gives the final answer.

questions.q: Look up the IP address of netrealm.io using a DNS query tool.
questions.hint: dig, nslookup or host + the domain.
questions.output:
;; ANSWER SECTION:
netrealm.io.     300   IN   A   203.0.113.42
;; Query time: 12 msec
;; SERVER: 192.168.1.1#53(192.168.1.1)
questions.explain: `dig` (or `nslookup`/`host`) queries DNS directly. The 300 is the TTL in seconds: how long resolvers may cache the answer.

questions.q: Using dig, look up the MAIL server (MX) records for netrealm.io.
questions.output:
;; ANSWER SECTION:
netrealm.io.   3600  IN  MX  10 mail1.netrealm.io.
netrealm.io.   3600  IN  MX  20 mail2.netrealm.io.
questions.explain: Add the record type: `dig netrealm.io MX`. Lower MX preference = tried first, so mail1 (10) beats mail2 (20).

questions.q: Show the router's active NAT translations.
questions.explain: Each PAT entry maps inside local IP:port ↔ inside global IP:port. Both hosts share 203.0.113.5 with different ports.

questions.q: Display all configured ACLs with their match counters.
questions.output:
Extended IP access list BLOCK_TELNET
    10 deny tcp any any eq telnet (37 matches)
    20 permit ip any any (10442 matches)
questions.explain: `show access-lists` (or `show ip access-lists`) shows every line and how many packets matched. Great for confirming an ACL is actually hit.

questions.q: Clients on this interface need DHCP from the server at 10.99.0.5 on another subnet. Configure the relay.
questions.explain: `ip helper-address` goes on the interface where the CLIENTS live. The router turns their broadcasts into unicasts to the server.

questions.q: Create standard ACL 10 that PERMITS the 192.168.1.0/24 network.
questions.explain: Standard ACLs use a wildcard mask: /24 → 0.0.0.255. Don't forget to apply it (`ip access-group 10 in/out` on an interface), and remember the implicit deny!

questions.q: Type the implicit statement at the end of every ACL (two words).
questions.explain: `deny any` (for extended ACLs, effectively `deny ip any any`). It's invisible but always there.

questions.q: An attacker floods a server with TCP SYNs and never completes the handshake. This is a:
questions.explain: Half-open connections fill the server's backlog. Mitigations include SYN cookies, rate limiting and upstream scrubbing.

questions.q: Besides UDP 53 for normal queries, when does DNS use TCP 53?
questions.explain: Zone transfers (AXFR/IXFR) and responses too large for UDP use TCP 53. DNSSEC has made TCP fallback more common.
